newsitem.title: ITALY: Left and right claim victory in Italian elections.
newsitem.headline: Left and right claim victory in Italian elections.

text.p: Both Italy's main political blocs claimed success on Monday from weekend local elections, which saw opposition parties lead in the key northern cities of Milan and Turin but gave government allies a boost in the provinces.
The big loser was the separatist Northern League, which lost control of Italy's second city, Milan, and was ousted from power from the three provincial governments it had previously run.

According to provisional results, the centre-right Freedom Alliance secured a first round lead in the most prestigious battles for mayors in the wealthy cities of Milan and Turin, pushing government coalition candidates into second place.
Both contests go to second round run-offs on May 11.
The governing centre-left Olive Tree coalition will have to work to win the support of its awkward parliamentary ally, the hard left Communist Refoundation, for the final showdown.

Refoundation stood its own candidates in both Milan and Turin securing around 10 percent of the vote, stronger than many analysts had expected. It immediately demanded concessions from Prime Minister Romano Prodi in return for its endorsement.

Party leader Fausto Bertinotti told Reuters he wanted Prodi to soften his stance on a planned reform of welfare spending, which many economists say is needed if Italy is to become a founder member of the European single currency.
"If we reach a clear agreement, we will be able to go to Milan and Turin and other cities and win," Bertinotti said.
Sunday's elections for mayors and local councils in more than 1,100 towns and cities marked the first big test for Prodi since he triumphed in last April's general election.
His coalition's popularity has taken a beating in recent months from resentment at tax hikes it has brought in to prepare the economy for the planned launch of the euro currency in 1999.

Nonetheless, the Olive Tree took the lead in mayoral races in the northeastern cities of Trieste and Pordenone, in the Adriatic port of Ancona and in Reggio Calabria on the toe of Italy. It also took the lead in two of the six elections for the president of provincial governments and won one outright.
"This is a success for Prodi," Luigi Manconi, leader of the Greens Party in his coalition, said in a statement.

But the centre-right also hailed the electoral results, especially in Milan, where industrialist Gabriele Albertini took around 41 percent of the vote, and in Turin, where candidate Raffaele Costa won around 43 percent.
"The Freedom Alliance has done even better than the rosiest of predictions," said Pierferdinando Casini, leader of the small centrist CCD party in the bloc.
Counting from the vote, for which 9.4 million voters -- or about one-fifth of the national electorate -- were eligible, began early on Monday with final results due later in the day.

But even before the full results were in, the Northern League was already counting the cost, after Marco Formentini, elected Milan mayor in 1993 at the height of the League's popularity, trailed in a poor third.
The result was a blow to the prestige of the League and a further sign of waning support for its separatist agenda.

Party leader Umberto Bossi, who blamed the defeat on southern Italian "immigrants" who had not supported the League, offered to step down, a tactic he has adopted in the past only to be reconfirmed in his position
"I would be very happy if the Northern League changed its secretary and left me free," Bossi said.
